title: Eid al-Fitr Prep Checklist: A Home Cleaning Countdown
seoTitle: Eid al-Fitr Prep Checklist: A Home Cleaning Countdown
excerpt: An Eid al-Fitr home cleaning checklist: a 14-day countdown schedule, priority areas, guest seating and storage zones, and family task assignments.
content: **An Eid al-Fitr prep checklist** usually falls apart not because anyone is lazy, but because every job gets crammed into the last three days. Washing curtains, scrubbing bathrooms, dusting ceilings, rearranging the living room, and filling cookie jars all pile up two days before Eid, tackled while fasting and while waiting for the first guests to arrive. The result is always half-done: the floors gleam but the guest bathroom still has limescale.

This page gives you a countdown schedule from 14 days out to the day before Eid, a breakdown of what to clean in each priority area, how to set up seating and storage for guests' belongings, plus a family task split, all with time estimates.

## The 14-Day Countdown Schedule

The principle is simple: dirty, wet jobs that need drying time come first, while anything instantly visible to the eye comes last. Reverse the order and the floor you mopped today gets dirty again tomorrow when you take down the dusty curtains.

A realistic split for a small to mid-size home with two working adults:

- **14 days out (2 hours):** Take down and wash every room's curtains plus the sofa cushion covers. In damp weather they need 1 to 2 days to dry.
- **13 to 11 days out (1 hour per day):** Sort the closets; move clothes untouched for a year into donation bags.
- **10 days out (1.5 hours):** Clean ceiling fans, AC vents, and AC filters. This dust will rain onto the furniture if you leave it for later.
- **8 days out (2 hours):** Deep clean the stove, the range hood or exhaust fan, and the wall behind the stove.
- **7 days out (1 hour):** Empty and clean the refrigerator, and wash the serving pieces that only come out once a year.
- **5 days out (2 hours):** Guest bathroom and main bathroom, including tile grout and drains.
- **4 days out (1 hour):** Sweep ceilings, wall corners, and door trim. Dusty work, still safe before the floors get their final pass.
- **3 days out (2 hours):** Wipe window glass, glass doors, mirrors, and picture frames.
- **2 days out (2 hours):** Rearrange the living room, set up extra seating, open the storage zone for guests' belongings.
- **1 day out (1.5 hours):** Mop every floor, empty the trash bins, put out fresh doormats, tidy the porch.
The total is about 16 hours. Split into one or two hour installments over two weeks, no single day ever feels heavy.
> **Practical tip:** Tape this schedule to the refrigerator door and cross off each finished item. Small installments are easy to forget when they only live in your head.
## Living Room: Where Guests Look the Longest
Guests sit here for 30 to 60 minutes looking around, so cobwebbed ceiling corners and a tangle of chargers will absolutely be noticed. Budget 3 to 4 hours, split into two sessions.

Work from top to bottom: ceiling corners and trim (15 minutes), ceiling fan or AC vents (30 minutes), rehang the freshly washed curtains (20 minutes), vacuum the sofa down into the deepest seat crevices (30 minutes), tables and display shelves (30 minutes), window glass (40 minutes), and finally the rug and floor (30 minutes).

The next problem is surfaces covered in everyday stuff: remotes, chargers, medicine, glasses, and toys. Apply the empty-surface rule: the coffee table only holds items that are genuinely on display, and everything else goes into closed bins under the table. One set of [Foldable Storage Bins](/product/foldable-storage-bins) is enough to swallow the kids' toys and small clutter, then folds flat once Eid is over.

For little handprints on the walls, a damp sponge with a drop of dish soap is all you need. Never take a rough scrub brush to interior paint; the finish peels and the scar stands out more than the stain did. To keep the tidiness going after Eid, follow the daily system in our [practical home organizing tips](/blog/tips-organizing-rumah-ala-indonesia).
## Kitchen: Clear It Before the Big Cooking Starts

The kitchen will get dirty again the moment the holiday cooking begins, so this cleanup is not about looks but about capacity: creating work space and storage space before the ingredients for rendang, opor, and the rest of the Eid feast pile up.

Start with the stove and range hood, because old grease takes the longest. Spray the greasy areas with hot water and dish soap, sprinkle baking soda on the caked spots, let it sit 20 minutes, then scrub with the coarse side of a sponge along the metal grain so you do not leave swirl scratches. Set aside 2 hours and keep a window open while you work.

The refrigerator gets its own session, about 1 hour. Empty everything, toss expired condiments, wipe the shelves with warm water and a splash of vinegar to kill odors, then restock by category: raw ingredients on the bottom shelf, cooked food in the middle, drinks in the door. Leave at least 40 percent of the shelving empty, because holiday pots and dessert containers will need the room. If your fridge always turns into a jumble, use grouping bins as shown in our [fridge organizer guide](/blog/organizer-kulkas).

Finally, pull out the gear that only appears at Eid: serving platters, soup bowls, the good glasses, and cookie jars. Rewash them a week out, not the day before, because the drying rack will be full and your everyday cookware will have nowhere to go. Check the rubber seal on every jar too: a hardened seal lets cookies go stale within two days.
## Guest Bathroom and Front Porch

The guest bathroom is the most forgotten area even though it will almost certainly be used. Set aside 2 hours to: scrub the toilet including under the seat, work the tile grout with an old toothbrush and diluted bleach (let it sit 10 minutes before scrubbing), dissolve limescale on the faucet and shower head with white vinegar, wipe the mirror, scrub the sink and tub, and flush the drains with hot water.

Once it is clean, stage the guest version: a dry bath mat, a full soap dispenser, clean towels, tissues, and a lidded trash can with a spare liner at the bottom. Keep backup soap and tissue in a small basket inside, so you are not running to the storage closet while the house is full. Shelving for wet areas is covered in our [bathroom storage ideas](/blog/ide-penyimpanan-kamar-mandi-agar-rapi).

The porch is the first impression and needs only 1 hour. Sweep dead leaves, scrub the floor with soap (moss in shaded spots is slippery and dangerous for elderly guests), wipe down planters, replace any dimming porch bulb, and dust off the railing.

The single biggest factor in porch tidiness is guests' shoes. Without a plan, shoes sprawl all the way to the front door within the first 15 minutes. Place a [5-Tier Minimalist Shoe Rack](/product/rak-sepatu-minimalis-5-tingkat) beside the door, and size its capacity by the number of guests arriving at once, not the number of people living in the house.
## Guest Seating and Belongings Storage

Start by counting your seating capacity. A three-seat sofa plus two armchairs means you seat five, while an extended-family visit can arrive eight to twelve strong. That gap is what you need to close, and it does not require buying a new sofa.

Three practical options: roll out a large area rug, around 6.5 by 10 feet, in front of the sofa with six to eight floor cushions (the most flexible, and kids get room too), keep four budget-friendly folding chairs stashed behind a closet, or borrow chairs from neighbors a week ahead. Arrange seating in a circle facing the center, not in rows facing the TV.

Guests' belongings are the next source of chaos: bags, coats, jackets, shoes, and gift baskets. Define the zones ahead of time and tell guests as they walk in. Set one large bin for bags and jackets in a corner near the door, wall hooks for coats, and the shoe rack on the porch. Without clear zones, bags end up on the sofa and the seating capacity you worked so hard to create shrinks instantly.

For the gift baskets and food gifts you receive, set up a transit area outside the living room, such as a spare bedroom or a kitchen corner. Left unchecked, the living room turns into a warehouse within two days.
> **Practical tip:** Gather the cookie jars on one large tray instead of lining them up directly on the table. When refills are needed, you lift one tray instead of shuttling seven jars.
## Divide the Work Among the Whole Family

The most common mistake: every job lands on one person, usually mom, who is simultaneously cooking for the big day. The fix is not more hustle; it is a written task list with names, days, and minute estimates.

A sensible split by age:

- **Kids 4 to 6 (15 minutes):** gather toys into a bin, line up slippers on the rack, empty small trash.
- **Kids 7 to 12 (20 to 30 minutes):** wipe tables and chairs, empty each room's trash bin, straighten books and magazines.
- **Teens (45 to 60 minutes):** wipe window glass, vacuum rugs and the sofa, lift light furniture during mopping.
- **Adults (1 to 2 hours per session):** stove and hood, bathrooms, ceilings, curtain washing, closet sorting.

Two rules make this split actually work. First, one person finishes one room completely; do not swarm from room to room, because that just produces a pile of half-done jobs. Second, use a 25-minute timer per session followed by a 5-minute break, especially while fasting.
## Frequently Asked Questions
### When is the right time to start cleaning the house for Eid?

Start 14 days out for anything that needs drying time, like curtains and sofa cushion covers. If you are starting only 3 days out, prioritize the guest bathroom, living room, and porch, and let go of areas guests never see, like the storage room.
### How do I clean years-old grease buildup on the range hood?

Spray it with hot water and dish soap, sprinkle baking soda over the crust, let it sit 20 minutes so the grease softens, then scrub along the metal grain. Thick buildup usually takes two rounds, so do it a week out rather than on the last day.
### Do curtains need washing, or is airing them out enough?

Thin curtains far from the kitchen can be aired out and gently brushed with a vacuum's brush nozzle. Heavy curtains, curtains near the kitchen, or curtains in a home facing a busy road should be washed, because dust and oil have soaked into the fibers.
### How do I keep guests' shoes from sprawling into the house?

Place the shoe rack beside the door before guests arrive, not after shoes have already piled up. If the rack fills, keep one empty foldable bin as overflow. Rack options for tight spaces are covered in our [ideas for shoe storage in a small closet](/blog/ideas-for-shoe-storage-in-small-closet).
### How should I store the jars and Eid gear once the holiday is over?

Wash and dry everything completely before storing, because trapped moisture molds the rubber seals within a month. Put it all in one bin labeled "Eid Supplies" on the top shelf, so next year you are not hunting through five different spots.
## Conclusion

The key to an Eid prep checklist is not working harder but working earlier and in the right order: dirty jobs first, visible polish last. Chip away starting 14 days out, focus on the areas guests actually see (living room, kitchen, guest bathroom, porch), set up seating and a belongings zone before the first guest arrives, and put the task split in writing so no one person carries it all.
